title: One canonical artifact per room, validated before hand-off
when: Every time a video project moves from one production room to the next.
summary: Each room emits exactly one schema-checked document that is the only contract the next room may read; rooms never pass loose notes or skip ahead.
steps: Assign one canonical artifact per room: research/niche -> research_brief; concept pitch -> proposal_packet; script -> script; scene & visual -> scene_plan; asset generation -> asset_manifest; editing -> edit_decisions; render -> render_report plus final_review; publish -> publish_log.

Declare each room in a data manifest (YAML/JSON): required input artifacts, optional inputs, produced artifacts, allowed tools, review focus items, success criteria, checkpoint_required, human_approval_default.
Before a room starts, confirm every required input exists and passes its JSON schema; refuse to start otherwise.
Before a room finishes, validate its output; a schema failure is a critical finding and blocks the hand-off.
Keep media files in typed folders (images, video, audio, music, renders) and reference them from artifacts by asset id so provenance survives.
Put room-specific extra fields inside a metadata object instead of inventing new top-level fields.
do: Let the orchestrator read the manifest instead of hard-coding stage order
Record provider, model, seed and cost on every generated asset
Create one workspace per video: artifacts/, assets/{images,video,audio,music}/, renders/, history/, snapshots/
avoid: Collapsing rooms (approved concept straight to bulk generation)
Writing files outside the project workspace where the dashboard cannot see them
Re-deciding upstream choices inside a downstream room (e.g. editing volumes during render)
checks: Completed and awaiting-approval rooms always carry their canonical artifact
Every artifact validates against its schema
Every cut source in edit_decisions resolves to an asset_manifest id with a real file path

title: Producer loop: pass, revise, or send back with hard limits
when: Running a full production where a later room can uncover a problem that was born in an earlier room.
summary: A stateful producer wraps stateless room workers, injects cumulative context, reviews every output, and either passes it, asks for a revision, or returns work to an earlier room, with caps that stop endless loops.
steps: Initialise producer state: pipeline, style, target duration, budget total/spent/remaining, artifact map, measured narration durations per section, style anchors, revision counts per room, issues log.
For each room run PREPARE (load the room skill, inject state and any feedback) -> RUN the worker -> REVIEW (schema, focus items, success criteria, style rules, cross-room checks) -> GATE.
Gate outcome PASS: store artifact, update totals (spend, durations, anchors).
Gate outcome REVISE: write structured feedback (reason, exact issue, constraint, what to keep, what to change, affected ids, budget left) and rerun the same room.
Gate outcome SEND_BACK: rerun an earlier room and invalidate every artifact after it; only for structural problems.
After the last room run a holistic QA (file probe, A/V sync, style consistency, budget reconciliation) and route each defect to the room able to fix it.
When any cap is reached, continue with logged warnings rather than blocking forever.
do: Absorb small drift (around +/-10% duration) downstream instead of re-running upstream
Pass style anchors (palette, character, lighting tokens) explicitly to the asset room
Reserve budget for assets and render before early rooms spend
avoid: Perfectionism loops
Sending back for cosmetic issues
Trusting metadata instead of probing the actual rendered file
checks: Revision count per room never exceeds the cap
Every send-back is logged with reason and target room
Budget alert raised when 90% is spent with rooms still pending
source: OpenMontage skills/pipelines/explainer/executive-producer.md; skills/pipelines/cinematic/executive-producer.md; skills/pipelines/hybrid/executive-producer.md; pipeline_defs/*.yaml orchestration blocks (AGPL-3.0, idea restated)

title: Append-only decision log keyed by category and subject
when: Any consequential choice is made or later changed: provider, voice, music, style, render engine, fallback, concept, extension, approval policy.
summary: Every meaningful choice is written down together with the options that lost and why; a change appends a new entry under the same key instead of editing history, giving both the user and the learning engine a truthful trail.
steps: Write each entry with: id, room, category, subject, options_considered (label, 0-1 score, reason or rejected_because), selected, reason, user_visible, user_approved, confidence 0-1.
Treat the (category, subject) pair as the identity of a decision; the newest entry for a pair is the current truth.
On change, append a new entry with the identical pair and move the previous pick into options_considered with a rejected_because explaining the change.

Use a fixed category list: pipeline, provider, renderer_family, render_runtime, composition_mode, playbook, fallback, budget_tradeoff, downgrade_approval, music_source, motion_commitment, concept, voice, capability_extension, playbook_override, visual_accuracy_check, approval_policy.
do: List at least two options for every decision, including unavailable ones with the reason
Write reasons tied to the brief, never filler
Calibrate confidence; provider picks usually involve trade-offs
avoid: Reasons like 'best option'
Every confidence at 1.0
Rewording the subject when revising (creates a phantom second decision)
Mutating old entries or only patching downstream artifacts
checks: Provider, style, music, voice, render engine and every downgrade each have an entry
No decision has a single option
Revised decisions reuse the exact category+subject

title: Delivery promise, motion ratio and no silent substitutions
when: At concept approval, before any paid call, when something breaks, and again at edit and render time.
summary: Classify what the video promises (e.g. real motion vs stills), announce every consequential tool choice before using it, ask before any major change, escalate blockers in a fixed format, and verify at the end that the promise survived.
steps: Record a delivery promise at concept time: promise type, motion_required, source_required, tone mode, quality floor (draft/presentable/broadcast), approved fallback (animatic, still-led, or none).
Before every paid or consequential generation, state tool, provider, model/variant, why it was chosen, and whether it is a sample or a batch.
Ask first before: switching provider or model family, moving from motion-led to still-led, changing render engine, dropping narration or music, moving from sample to batch.

On a blocker report five things: what was tried, what failed, failure class (auth / provider access / tool bug / prompt or design quality), the options, and a recommended option with reasoning; then wait.
At edit time compute motion ratio = cuts with real motion (video or animation) / total cuts and compare with the promise minimum.
At render time confirm the engine that actually ran equals the engine locked at concept and that no silent downgrade happened.
do: When asking the user to choose: give a shortlist, short trade-offs, one recommendation, then wait
For a faceless channel decide up front if the format is motion-led (stock/generated video b-roll) or still-led (images with pan/zoom)
avoid: Quietly turning a motion promise into a pan-and-zoom slideshow
Running a substitute path before the user approves it
Hiding degraded paths in the final output
checks: Motion ratio meets the promise minimum
final_review records runtime_swap_detected=false and silent_downgrade_detected=false
Every substitution has a logged, user-approved decision

title: Resolve the music plan at concept time, not at asset time
when: During concept approval for any video that has an audio bed.
summary: Music is surfaced as an explicit choice before anything is generated, executed exactly as approved later, and trimmed to its strongest section so a video never ends up silent or with a weak intro by surprise.
steps: Check sources in order: the user's own music library, royalty-free search providers, music generation, bring-your-own drop folder.
Present explicit options (library track X, search, provide own, generate with named provider and cost, proceed without music) and record the choice with path or prompt seed.
If no source exists, say so at concept time, not later.
In the asset room execute exactly the recorded plan; changing source later is a major change that needs approval.

For a chosen track, analyse per-second loudness and start playback at the highest-energy window that is as long as the video, skipping quiet intros; enable looping if the remaining track is shorter than the video.
Make sure the music covers the full video duration.
do: Treat music as a timing grid to cut to, not a sweetener added at render
Generate a short music sample before committing when using generation
avoid: Assuming a 'pure' silent piece will work
Generating a track because the edit 'feels thin' after the user chose none
Music at full volume under narration
checks: Music decision present in the concept artifact
Rendered file has an audio stream with audible music unless explicitly opted out

title: Human approval gates, live progress and resume
when: On entering, during, and on finishing any room, and on restarting an interrupted project.
summary: Each room writes a live in-progress checkpoint, saves partial progress per scene, and, when the manifest says the room is gated, stops with a clear approval request; approval only ever covers that one gate.
steps: Read checkpoint_required and human_approval_default for the room from the manifest; treat the flag as binding.
On entry write status in_progress; during long rooms (assets, render) refresh partial progress with completed scene ids after each unit.
When gated: write awaiting_human and present artifact summary, review results (criticals fixed, open suggestions), cost so far and projected, and the action needed; then stop all further work.
Approve -> rewrite as completed with human_approved=true; Revise -> rerun the room with the feedback, re-review, re-checkpoint (superseded version archived to history); Abort -> stop.
Count a blanket 'do everything' only if it is logged as an approval_policy decision at the moment it is given.
Hold the asset gate on a per-scene filmstrip (thumbnails, stills, waveforms), never on a rendered draft; rendering belongs to the next room.
On restart compute the next room; if it is in_progress, resume from partial progress and skip completed units; if awaiting_human, re-present.
do: Always checkpoint expensive work even if not strictly required
Show spend and remaining budget at every approval request
avoid: Presenting and continuing in the same step
Treating an early 'looks great' as approval for later gates
Destroying superseded versions
checks: A gated room cannot be marked completed without human_approved=true
Every completed/awaiting checkpoint embeds the room artifact
History folder contains every superseded checkpoint
source: OpenMontage skills/meta/checkpoint-protocol.md; schemas/checkpoints/checkpoint.schema.json; AGENT_GUIDE.md (Human Checkpoint Protocol) (AGPL-3.0, idea restated)

title: Sample first, batch second
when: Before generating any expensive asset type in bulk, and before full production of a reference-inspired video.
summary: Produce one cheap, representative sample per costly asset type (and a short preview clip for reference-driven work), get approval, then lock those exact settings for the batch.
steps: For reference-driven videos build a 10-15 s preview: the opening hook plus one representative middle scene with real voice, real visuals, a music snippet and the caption style.
For narration, sample the section with the most demanding delivery (not automatically the first).
For images or clips, sample the most representative scene (in batches, the visual peak / hero scene).
For generated music, sample a short clip to confirm mood and energy.
If rejected, change the specific parameter (voice, prompt, provider) and resample; after 3 rounds escalate to the user for a decision.
Record the approved sample path and exact settings in the asset manifest; any later change of provider, voice, speed or model requires a new sample.
do: Tell the user the sample cost against the projected full cost
Name tool, provider and model before sampling
avoid: Skipping the sample because the user said 'just do it' (advise once, then respect insistence)
Batching with settings that differ from the approved sample
checks: Batch settings equal approved sample settings
Sample approval recorded before batch

title: Critiques must be accurate, complete and constructive
when: Writing any review finding for any room.
summary: A finding names a problem; a critique tells the next room exactly how to fix it. Each critique points at a concrete location, sweeps for siblings of the same mistake, and, when critical, carries a ready-to-apply fix.
steps: Accurate: cite the artifact field, script line, timestamp or frame; if you cannot point to it, you are guessing and must not file it.
Complete: after finding one problem, scan the rest of the artifact for the same class of problem before returning.
Constructive: every critical finding carries a proposed_fix (replacement text, exact value or specific action); every suggestion carries a proposed_change.
If no concrete fix can be proposed, file it as 'investigation' instead of critical so it does not block.
do: Good: 'Section 3 holds about 180 words in a 10 s window (~1,080 wpm); cut to about 25 words.'
Good: 'Hook asks a question without urgency; lead with the counter-intuitive stat from key point 2.'
avoid: Vague findings such as 'script may be too long' or 'hook is weak'
Inflating severity: a required field missing is critical, a wordy paragraph is only a suggestion, a typo is a nitpick
Reviewing the process instead of the output
checks: Every finding has a location reference
No critical without a fix
Sibling sweep performed after each critical

title: Per-room self-review and pass/revise decision
when: After any room produces its artifact and before checkpointing.
summary: Load the room's focus items, success criteria, style rules and taste dials, validate schema, grade findings by severity, then pass, revise, or pass with warnings after the round cap.
steps: Load: manifest review_focus and success_criteria for the room, active style quality rules, taste profile, the artifact.
Validate the artifact schema; failure is critical and must be fixed immediately.
Evaluate each focus item and assign critical / suggestion / nitpick / investigation.
Cross-check style: palette colours used, transitions inside the allowed set, holds inside min/max, style cues present in asset prompts, quality rules respected; each violation is a suggestion.
Check taste dials against layout variety, pacing, callout density and prompts.
Check each success criterion (yes / no / partial); any unmet criterion is critical.
Decide: 0 critical -> PASS (note suggestions); >=1 critical -> REVISE then re-review; still critical after the round cap -> PASS_WITH_WARNINGS and log unresolved items.

Record: room, round, decision, numbered findings with description, action, status (pending/fixed/accepted/deferred), and totals (critical fixed, suggestions, nitpicks, style violations, criteria met N/M).
do: Use room-specific emphasis: research = source diversity and verifiability; concept = delivery promise, engine choice, music/voice plan; script = timing, arc, cue density; scene plan = coverage, variety, feasibility, slideshow risk; assets = files exist, style consistency, budget; edit = coverage, sync, subtitles, promise; render = playable, duration, audio; publish = metadata completeness
avoid: Blocking indefinitely
Treating style rules as optional
checks: Schema validated first
All success criteria explicitly scored
Review record stored with the checkpoint
source: OpenMontage skills/meta/reviewer.md (Protocol, Stage-Specific Review Guidance); schemas/artifacts/review.schema.json (AGPL-3.0, idea restated)

title: Severity ladder with concrete triggers
when: Assigning severity to any finding in any room.
summary: Four levels (critical, suggestion, nitpick, investigation) with a fixed list of what always counts as critical so reviewers stay consistent across videos.
steps: CRITICAL (must fix before proceeding): invalid schema; unmet success criterion; wrong facts about a reference video; concept is a near copy of the reference; spend over estimate by more than 30% without re-approval; render engine or creative grammar changed without a logged decision; render produced without a final review; silent motion-to-still downgrade; slideshow risk verdict fail; scene variation verdict fail; two scenes sharing the same primary visual subject (hero spine); captions duplicating on-screen text; user-supplied media not actually inspected; plan relies on content the source does not contain; publishing with a non-passing final review.

SUGGESTION (should fix, does not block): style-rule violation; weak or surface-only differentiation from a reference; something the user said they loved got dropped; slideshow verdict revise; scenes missing shot intent; decision with one option; all confidences 1.0; new assets beyond the approved plan; missing taste profile on low-stakes work; taste-dial violations that do not break the promise.
NITPICK (optional polish): small wording, minor timing nudges.
INVESTIGATION: a real concern without a concrete fix; surfaced for the next round, never blocking.
do: Escalate repeated suggestions of the same class across videos into a learning candidate
avoid: Marking taste opinions as critical
Leaving style violations unflagged because the result 'looks fine'
checks: Each critical maps to one of the listed triggers or a manifest success criterion
source: OpenMontage skills/meta/reviewer.md (Steps 3-6, Reference Alignment, Decision Log, Source Understanding, Final Self-Review, Composition Authoring Mode reviews) (AGPL-3.0, idea restated)

title: Slideshow-risk and scene-variation scoring
when: After the scene plan is written and again after the edit decisions exist.
summary: Two structural scores (0-5, lower is better) predict whether the video will feel like animated slides; the edit must never score worse than the scene plan.
steps: Slideshow risk = mean of six dimensions, each 0-5.
Repetition: +2 if one scene type exceeds 70% of scenes; +1.5 if fewer than 60% of scene descriptions are unique (first 50 characters); +1.5 if one shot size exceeds 60%; cap 5.
Decorative visuals: share of scenes with no information role, narrative role or shot intent x 5.
Weak motion: among scenes with camera movement, share lacking shot intent x 4 (no movement at all scores 1.5).
Weak shot intent: (1 - share of scenes with shot intent) x 5.
Typography over-reliance: text/stat/KPI scene share >60% -> 4, >40% -> 2.5, >20% -> 1, else 0.
Unsupported cinematic claim (only when the style claims cinematic): +1.8 each for no hero moment, <30% scenes with camera movement, <30% scenes with a lighting key.
Verdict: average <2 strong, <3 acceptable, <4 revise (suggestion; name dimensions >=3.5), >=4 fail (critical; do not render).

Variation check (scene plan): each violation adds 0.6 (cap 5), same verdict bands. Violations: one shot size >50% of scenes; a run of >=3 identical shot sizes; >60% static or unspecified movement (aim for >=40% moving); <=1 lighting setup across >=4 scenes; no hero moment; hero shares shot size with a neighbour; >=30% of descriptions contain generic words; <30% scenes with texture keywords; <50% scenes with shot intent.
Recompute at edit time with real cuts; if the score rose versus the scene plan, flag it.
do: Treat the generic-word list as the 'lazy description' detector: a person, a beautiful, modern, futuristic, cutting-edge, sleek, innovative, state-of-the-art, next-generation, revolutionary, dynamic, vibrant, stunning, breathtaking, amazing, incredible, powerful, seamless
avoid: Mixing score directions; keep lower = better everywhere (the source reviewer text and checker disagree on naming)
checks: Scene-plan slideshow verdict is not fail before assets are generated
Edit-stage score <= scene-plan score

title: Inspect the actual render before anyone sees it
when: Immediately after every render, before presenting or publishing.
summary: Five mandatory checks on the real file (probe, frames, audio, promise, subtitles) plus a transcript comparison produce a pass/revise/fail status and a routed next action.
steps: Technical probe first: valid container, duration within tolerance, resolution and fps as planned, audio stream present (if missing, stop and fix), non-trivial file size.

Visual spot-check: sample at least 4 frames (opening, middle, climax, ending) or one per cut midpoint; look for black frames, broken overlays, missing assets, unreadable or stretched content, wrong background, captions over faces, wrong CTA text.

Audio spot-check: transcribe the rendered file; zero words means silent audio (stop); fewer than 80% of script words means cut-off; last spoken word should equal last scripted word; music audible; no clipping; no unexpected silence.
Promise preservation: engine used equals engine locked; motion ratio recorded; no silent downgrade.
Subtitle check: expected vs present, coverage ratio, timing drift.
Set status pass / revise / fail and recommended_action: present_to_user, re_render, revise_edit, revise_assets, block, re_author.
Never present a revise or fail render as finished; never publish without a pass.
do: Write a short post-render report: file facts, audio completeness (N/M words), scenes inspected, captions, issues with severity, recommendations
avoid: Checking frames but skipping the audio transcript (most common miss)
Fixing problems by changing edit values inside the render step
checks: final_review artifact exists next to render_report
All five checks have data
Publish room receives final_review with status pass

title: Distinctness review: no hero spine, no recycled look
when: Before approving a scene plan and before approving any flagship render.
summary: Record one representative frame and the primary visual subject per scene, reject scenes that share a subject, keep the signature visual scarce, and ask whether the video could belong to any other channel.
steps: Inventory each scene: primary visual subject plus a representative (mid-scene) frame.
If two or more scenes share the same primary subject (the same hero object merely re-captioned) mark critical and re-plan those scenes.
Confirm the declared signature device appears in at least one beat but only in one or two beats, not as scaffolding for most scenes.

Answer explicitly: could this video belong to any other channel or topic after swapping the title? Does it reuse a look from a previous video of ours? A yes to either means re-author the art direction.

Caption/on-screen text dedup: decide once per video whether captions add meaning (numbers, names, translations, attributions) or echo the narration for accessibility; never show the same line twice at the same moment.
A missing recorded answer is itself a critical finding.
do: Store each video's art-direction summary so the next review can compare against past looks
avoid: The same striking object in every scene with different text underneath (branded slides)
Captions that repeat the headline already on screen
checks: Scene inventory recorded
Distinctness questions answered in the review record
No caption/on-screen duplicate windows

title: Tells of boring, lazy and amateur videos (with fixes)
when: Any review of scene plans, edits or renders; also usable as a pre-flight checklist for each room.
summary: A consolidated catalogue of the failure patterns the source repeatedly warns about, grouped into boring (rhythm), lazy (thinking) and amateur (craft), each paired with its standard fix.
steps: BORING -> fix: identical hold lengths -> vary by tone table and hero status; same transition on every cut -> small vocabulary used deliberately; >3 consecutive scenes of one type -> alternate dense and breathing scenes; >60% text cards -> add visual scenes; >60% static shots -> purposeful movement in >=40%; no hero moment -> mark and protect 2-3 heroes; no dynamics -> one held silence, quiet vs impact moments; music added at the end -> cut to the music grid.

LAZY -> fix: generic adjectives in prompts -> concrete subject, light, texture, era; the same style prefix pasted into every prompt -> adapt anchors per scene; category queries like 'home' -> concrete nouns (door, key, mat); picking the top score -> judge era, motion, adjacency, register; one query per slot -> 2-3 queries; three re-titled versions of one concept -> different structures and insights; hooks built from a template first -> write in own words, then sharpen; 'read naturally' voice notes -> pace, pause and emphasis cues; 'in this video we will...' openers -> open on the most surprising finding.

AMATEUR -> fix: freeze-frame endings -> fade to black; wipes, zoom blurs, RGB splits, light leaks, glitch in a documentary register -> hard cuts and few dissolves; mixed-source footage left ungraded -> one LUT across the timeline; low-res clips upscaled -> letterbox/pillarbox; captions duplicating on-screen text or covering faces -> dedupe, lower 20% placement; AI images containing exact text (CTA, names, numbers) -> render text natively; music at full volume under narration -> ducking; cuts mid-word or audio pops -> cut on word boundaries with handles; black gaps between scenes -> continuous coverage; three different transition types in the first 15 s or a dissolve on every cut -> commit to hard cuts; loudness jumps between sections -> normalise; letterbox added only to look cinematic -> use only when it helps.
do: Attach the matching fix text automatically when the reviewer detects a tell
avoid: Masking a weak edit with extra graphics, narration or transitions
checks: Each tell is checked at the room where it is cheapest to fix

title: When to redo one scene versus a whole room, and where to route defects
when: A review or final QA finds a defect and the system must choose the smallest effective redo.
summary: Most defects are fixed by redoing a single slot or scene in the room that owns it; whole-room reruns are reserved for structural failures, and every redo excludes previously rejected candidates.
steps: Single-slot retrieval redo: best match score below 0.22 -> rewrite queries and grow the candidate pool for that slot only (max 2 growth passes), then drop the slot or ask the user for footage.
Adjacency redo: two neighbouring picks share subject and scale, or the diversity pass drops one -> re-rank that slot excluding the surviving twin.
Narration overrun for one section: if actual audio exceeds plan by more than 15% but no more than 25%, stretch that scene; above that, send only that section back to script with a word cap.
Image/clip mismatch: refine the prompt specifically (not an identical retry), max 2 retries, then escalate.
Hero frame failure: regenerate using the pre-caption / critique / post-caption method.
Clip too short for its hold: slow to 0.5-0.75x only on near-static footage, or borrow time from the next slot, or swap in the #2 candidate from the rejected list.
Weak final image: swap in a stronger candidate; the tail is remembered disproportionately.
Caption over a face or unreadable text in a frame: re-render with corrected placement.
Decorative scene (no role or intent) or shared primary subject: re-plan those scenes only.
Whole-room redo only for: schema failure, slideshow verdict fail, variation fail, structural duration miss, wrong concept.

Route by defect type: audio mix -> render; visual quality -> assets (regenerate) or scene plan (re-plan); duration -> script; A/V sync -> edit; text or diagram sharpness -> render or assets; motion or timing -> edit (re-time) or scene plan; factual error -> script then cascade forward.
do: Keep a global exclude list so the same asset never wins two slots
Log every rejected pick with its score and reason so the next redo can reach for #2
avoid: Re-running the entire asset batch for one bad scene
Forcing a best-of-a-bad-bunch pick
checks: Each redo targets the smallest owning unit
Rejected candidates are excluded on rerun

title: Taste profile: design read plus three 1-10 dials
when: Before choosing a style, palette or composition approach for a video, and whenever a flagship episode needs its own look.
summary: Taste is expressed as a short, specific design read plus three numeric dials (visual variance, motion intensity, information density), palette discipline, layout variation, reference strategy, anti-patterns and quality gates; every downstream room is checked against it.
steps: Write the design read: what the video must feel like and why, tied to audience, promise, platform and subject. Adjective lists ('modern, clean, cinematic') are rejected.

Set visual_variance (low = tight repeated grammar; mid = a few purposeful scene families; high = each beat may change mode), motion_intensity (low = calm holds, small transitions; mid = clear accents and reveals; high = fast kinetic, frequent direction changes), information_density (low = one idea per frame; mid = main idea plus support; high = dense diagrams/dashboards).

Apply interactions: high motion + low density -> short kinetic beats; low motion + high density -> stable frames, chart builds, long readable holds; high variance -> add anchors (recurring type, palette, framing or sound motif).
Choose a style path: an existing preset if it honestly fits; a custom style file for a subject with its own visual world; one-off art direction for flagship work.
Plan references: a reference frame for each family of similar scenes or key moment (never a single mood board standing in for everything); inspect real product/brand surfaces before styling them.

Carry downstream: scene plan varies layouts by variance, caps text by density, picks transitions and camera moves by motion; assets include palette, texture, framing and reference in prompts; edit matches hold length and rhythm to the motion dial.

Run the anti-default checklist: stock AI-purple gradients or default corporate blue that the subject does not justify; one transition type everywhere while variance is 4+; kinetic motion that fights narration; dense callouts when density <=4; text-only slides unless typography is the concept; attractive mood boards that map to no scene family; brand videos that never show the real product.
do: Use the 'swap the title' test: if the video could fit any topic after changing the title, the taste direction is too generic
avoid: Letting preset availability override the design read
Missing taste profile on flagship work (critical) — on low-stakes work it is only a suggestion
checks: taste_profile present in concept artifact

On-screen text density within the density dial

title: Bespoke versus templated composition and the scarce signature device
when: Deciding how a video's visuals are built: assembled from reusable scene templates or authored fresh.
summary: Borrow technical know-how freely but never borrow a previous look; templates are right for batch/series consistency, fresh art direction is right for flagship pieces, and a single signature visual should appear only in one or two climactic beats.
steps: Lock three separate choices at concept time: creative grammar (what kind of video), render engine, authoring mode (templated vs bespoke).
Use templated for batch output, translated variants, quick drafts and low-stakes clips; use bespoke for launches, flagship explainers, brand pieces; tell the user bespoke costs more effort.
Before building bespoke, write the art direction: palette, type personality, motion character, layout system, one signature device unique to this piece.

Apply motion principles (anticipation, staging, follow-through, slow in/out, arcs, timing, exaggeration, appeal) rather than stock presets; layer two to four separate motion ideas in each beat and vary easing, with three or more distinct curves per video; reserve heavy GPU-style effects for 1-3 hero beats.

Make rendering deterministic: seeded randomness, scene-local timing.

title: Automatic colour, contrast and type-scale validation
when: Creating or loading any style file, and as a pre-render accessibility gate.
summary: Deterministic checks for text contrast, colour-blind confusion, palette harmony, type scale and weight hierarchy turn 'looks good' into pass/fail numbers.
steps: Contrast ratio = (L_lighter + 0.05) / (L_darker + 0.05) with sRGB relative luminance (0.2126 R + 0.7152 G + 0.0722 B on linearised channels).

Body text on background must reach 4.5 (error below; info if below 7). Muted text must reach 3.0 (error below; warning if below 4.5). Overlay text vs overlay background, compositing any alpha onto the page background first.

Colour-blind check: for each pair of saturated colours (saturation >=0.15) whose lightness differs by <=0.3, flag if their hues fall into known confusion ranges for red-green (deutan/protan) or blue-yellow (tritan) vision.
Harmony generation from a base hue: complementary 0/180, analogous -30/0/+30, triadic 0/120/240, split-complementary 0/150/210.
Type scale from base size b and ratio r: caption b/r, body b, subheading b*r, heading b*r^2, display b*r^3; video base 24 px; caption under 16 px is a warning; ratio under 1.1 is too tight.
Hierarchy: heading weight above body weight, ideally by >=200; stat-card size multiplier >1 (>=2 for video); weight matrix must not increase from title -> heading -> body -> caption.
Overall pass = zero errors.

title: Five-aspect shot breakdown (subject, motion, scene, framing, camera)
when: Describing any shot: analysing a competitor/reference video, writing a scene plan, or writing a generation prompt.
summary: Every shot is described along five fixed aspects in a fixed order with overlays kept as a separate layer and every non-applicable aspect explicitly marked N/A, so analysis output can be lifted straight into plans and prompts.
steps: Subject: type, count, attributes (age, role, clothing, distinguishing marks), how to tell multiple subjects apart, and how subjects change across shots (revealed, disappearing, switching, alternating).
Subject motion: actions in time order; interactions (parallel, sequential, reactive); body locomotion vs gesture vs facial.

Scene: overlays listed separately (titles, lower-thirds, graphics, watermarks); point of view (for example aerial or drone, top-down, macro, over-the-shoulder, handheld, tripod/locked-off, FPV, dashcam); the location; the time of day; environmental dynamics such as weather, particles or crowds.

Spatial framing: how big the subject is in frame (extreme close-up through extreme wide), where it sits, which depth layers are used (front/middle/back), whether the camera is above, level with or below it, and how each of these shifts during the shot.

Camera: playback speed (real-time, slow motion, time-lapse), lens character (anamorphic, fisheye, tilt-shift), height, angle (high, low, Dutch), focus/depth of field (rack, deep, shallow), stability (tripod, gimbal, handheld), and any move (pan, tilt, push-in, pull-out, dolly, truck, crane, orbit).
Write N/A explicitly for anything absent (e.g. 'Camera: N/A, native motion-graphics scene').

title: Turn a reference video into reusable DNA without copying it

Replication guidance: 3-5 elements that make it work, elements needing custom work, complexity, whether motion is required, 3-5 differentiation seeds, style customisations.

title: Word budget, narrative arc and visual cue density
when: Writing or reviewing a narration script for a target duration.
summary: Size the script from speaking rate and duration, structure it as hook-setup-build-climax-landing with causal links, and embed a visual cue roughly every 8-10 seconds so the scene room always knows what to show.
steps: Choose a rate: conversational ~150 wpm, contemplative ~120, energetic ~180, technical ~130, mood/cinematic ~120, long-form YouTube 150-160.
Producer check: estimated minutes = words / 150; above 1.15 x target -> cut N words; below 0.7 x target -> add content; aim within +/-10%.

Leave air: narration should fill 85-90% of the video; budget 2.0-2.5 words/s for calm delivery and 2.5-3.0 for energetic; allocate words per scene by duration (a 5 s scene ~10-12 words); keep 0.5-1 s of silence at scene changes; keep the first and last scenes light.

Arc: hook 0-5 s (question, bold claim, surprising fact); setup 5-15 s (why care, open a knowledge gap); build with 'therefore' / 'but' links, one key point per section; climax a few seconds before the end delivering the hook's promise; landing in the last ~5 s with the core message and CTA, no new information.

Add pronunciation guides for jargon, acronyms and names.
Trace every factual claim to the research; never invent numbers, dates or attributions.

'And then' sequencing
Introducing new information in the landing

title: Retention pacing for long-form YouTube and Shorts
when: Pacing a faceless YouTube long-form episode or a vertical short.
summary: Long-form survives the first 30 seconds and the 2-3 minute valley with early payoffs, scheduled pattern interrupts and re-hooks; shorts hook within 1-2 seconds and change something every 1-3 seconds; both target -14 LUFS.
steps: Long-form structure: intro hook + stakes + preview complete by 0:30; first real payoff before 2:00; chapters of 2-4 minutes (max 5-6 chapters in 10-15 min); a re-hook around 2:00 then every 3-4 minutes; a short palette-cleanser between heavy chapters; CTA and end screen in the last 20 s.

Long-form interrupts: minor (b-roll change, graphic, angle shift) every 20-30 s; major (music change, burst of 5-10 quick cuts over 10-15 s) every 60-90 s, with one placed around 1:45-2:00; open loops in the first 60 s resolved later.

Long-form audio: continuous bed ducked 18-20 dB below speech, crossfades of 2-3 s between sections, BPM kept within +/-10 across the video, -14 LUFS integrated, chapter-to-chapter variation under 2 LU, limiter around -1.5 dBTP.

Shorts: 9:16, universal safe zone about 900x1400 centred (bottom ~300 px is platform UI), hook in the first 1-2 s, on-screen text within 0.5 s, voice starts immediately, movement on frame 1, a visual change every 1-3 s (20-40 cuts per minute), text blocks held 2-4 s, no static hold over 3 s, captions mandatory at 42 px or larger, -14 LUFS and -1 dBTP.

title: Documentary montage brief and beat/hold math
when: Planning a footage-led, music-driven montage or b-roll sequence where meaning comes from juxtaposition.
summary: Name one thematic question, one emotional register and one shape; derive slot count and hold lengths from a tone table; protect hero slots; close with a short philosophical end tag.
steps: Write the thematic question as one sentence that carries a feeling (not a topic, not a shot list).
Choose one register: elegiac, urgent, reverent, wry, dreamlike.
Cap beats by duration: 30-45 s -> 8-12 cuts; 60-90 s -> 15-25; 2-3 min -> 30-50.

Choose a shape: single-image expansion (one idea from many angles, best under 60 s), before/after (half, a pivot slot, half), three-act setup/turn/release (30/40/30, needs >90 s), list/catalogue (accumulation, no arc).
Slots ~= duration / base hold from the tone table; mark at least 2 hero slots (opening, turn, final image).
Hero slots get the max hold, 3 queries and bigger candidate pools; cutaways get the base hold; quick passes get the min.
Sum of target holds must land within +/-10% of the duration; if over, compress non-hero holds first, never heroes.
Music is mandatory unless the user explicitly opts out with a reason; narration is optional and off by default; generated clips are off by default.

title: Slot descriptions, stock queries and retrieval-first picking
when: Filling b-roll slots from stock/archive footage instead of generating clips.
summary: Describe each slot as a concrete photograph, write 2-3 short search queries, build a candidate pool 8-12 times larger than the slot count, rank by the description, pick by judgement, diversify neighbours and log every rejection.
steps: Write each slot description like a stock tag string: subject, action/pose, environment, lighting, era/texture hint; nouns and adjectives only, no emotion words, no intentions. Test: can you picture one specific photograph?
Write 2-3 queries per slot of 2-5 words: a literal query, a lateral query (other angle or scale), and for hero slots an association query.

Assign preferred sources by era and subject (modern HD stock for people/cities/nature; public-domain archives for vintage texture; space agencies for scale; ocean agencies for underwater); for vintage briefs use period vocabulary and send >=60% of slots to archive sources.
Build the pool: de-duplicate queries, fan out per source group, 4-8 results per query per source, pool size 8-12 x slot count, filter by min duration 3 s, max 40 s, landscape, min width 1280.
Sanity-check the pool: at least 50 rows, no skew against the brief's era, average motion not near zero (otherwise you are building a slideshow).
Rank each slot on its description (not its queries), excluding already-picked ids, with a minimum motion filter; hero slots look at 30 candidates, others 12.
Pick by judgement among the top 3-5: era fit, motion fit for the hold, compositional carry next to neighbours, emotional register; score never overrides tone.
Score bands (CLIP-style cosine): >=0.30 usually usable; 0.22-0.30 needs judgement; <0.22 grow the pool (max 2 growth passes) or drop/replace the slot.
Run a diversity pass over the picks in timeline order; if one is dropped, re-rank that slot excluding its twin.
Record provider, original URL, licence, score and a one-line retrieval summary per asset; log rejected high-score picks with reasons.

Run search downloads in parallel with narration and music work

Picking by score alone
Forgetting the exclude list so one great clip wins every slot
Unbounded pool growth

title: Montage edit rules: rhythm, juxtaposition, music sync, restraint
when: Cutting a footage-led montage or a b-roll heavy segment to music.
summary: Arrange by narrative beat not score, trim each clip to its best moment with handles, cut to the music grid with one deliberate silence, use at most four transitions, enforce adjacent diversity, weld hard transitions with L-cuts, and give every cut a written reason.
steps: Before cutting, re-read the brief; adding narration, swapping music or stretching duration are major changes that need approval.
Set the rhythm grid from the tone table: heroes get max hold, cutaways base, quick passes min.
Keep the planned slot order; reorder only to land a hero on a downbeat, to break visual monotony, or to replace a weak final image; log every reorder with a reason.
Trim to the best sub-window (a 12 s clip usually holds one 3 s moment), end before the action finishes (on a look, not a move-off), keep 4-6 frames of handle at each end.
If a clip is too short: slow to 0.5-0.75x only for near-static shots, or borrow time from the next slot, or use the #2 candidate; never freeze the last frame.
Music sync: hero cuts on downbeats (without beat data, every 4 s at 60 bpm); one held silence of about 2 s at the emotional centre for pieces of 60 s or more; music fades under the last 3-5 s.

Transitions: hard cut by default; dissolve 0.5-1.0 s for emotionally related shots or time passing; fade to black 0.5 s at act breaks or once near the end; fade in/out 0.5-1.0 s as bookends; maximum four distinct types.
Adjacent diversity walk: no two neighbours with the same subject and scale; break same-palette runs at least every 4 cuts; flip or reorder same-direction motion.
L-cuts: carry strong ambient sound (rain, footsteps, traffic) 0.5-1.5 s under the next shot on the 3-4 hardest transitions.
End tag overlay offset = body duration - tag duration so their fade-outs align.
Write a one-line reason for every cut; if none exists, the cut is arbitrary.

Swap a weak final image for a stronger one (the last frame is remembered most)
avoid: Wipes, push/slide, zoom blur, RGB split, light leaks, glitch in this register
Dissolves on every cut
Three transition types in the first 15 s
Cutting by information density instead of rhythm
Freeze-frame endings

<=4 transition types

title: Register smoothing at render: one canvas, one grade, one mix
when: Rendering a timeline built from footage of mixed sources, eras and resolutions.
summary: Make clips from different sources feel like one film by forcing one canvas and letterbox, one colour grade across the whole timeline, and one audio mix executed exactly as the edit specified, then verify the actual file.
steps: Resolve the canvas from the platform: vertical 1080x1920 (centre-crop 16:9), YouTube 1920x1080 (optional 2.35:1 bars = about 140 px top and bottom), professional networks 1920x1080.
Letterbox or pillarbox low-resolution clips instead of upscaling them.

Apply a single LUT at timeline level chosen by tone: warm film (elegiac, dreamlike), cool archive (urgent, wry), neutral documentary (reverent), bleach bypass (harsh, wry); fall back to neutral with a warning; never grade clip by clip.
Mix once: music at the edit's level with its fades; silence window ducked to zero with a 0.2 s hold-off on the way back; L-cut ambience at 0.5-0.7 under the music; no narration unless approved.
Encode: H.264, yuv420p, CRF 18, 24 fps without up-converting (drop frames evenly, never blend), AAC 192 kbps.
Normalise exotic source containers before the render; split very long renders and stitch.

Verify the file: duration within 0.5 s of plan, resolution equals canvas, audio stream present, first frame is the fade-in, last frame black or the end tag, silence visible in the waveform, end-tag text visible over footage (not over black).

Stop and ask if a required element (music, end tag) is missing

Adjusting edit values inside the render call
Adding ambience 'to fill the gap'

title: Mood-led pieces: emotional arc, hero frames and restraint

steps: Classify what material really exists (only footage; footage with some stills; mostly stills; generated inserts supporting real footage; a mixed montage) and whether motion is a hard requirement.

Beat map: hook, escalation, reveal, landing (+ one midpoint turn if longer); never reveal the best moment early.

title: Mining a ranked batch of standalone shorts from a long video

title: Lesson-to-skill loop: capture, distil, trial, promote, version, retire
when: After every finished video (and after analytics arrive), to turn repeated findings and user corrections into tested, versioned skills.
summary: OpenMontage provides the raw materials (audit logs, review findings, rejected picks, prompt triplets, project-scoped skills, promotion suggestions); this loop adds explicit thresholds, a trial phase, versioning and retirement so the engine actually improves from its own work.
steps: CAPTURE per video: review findings with severity and disposition, producer revisions and send-backs, decision-log revisions (especially user overrides), rejected picks with reasons, sample rejections, prompt pre/critique/post triplets, final review status and issues, user free-text feedback at each gate, later channel analytics (CTR, average view duration, retention dips by timestamp).
DISTIL: cluster findings by category + room + root cause; write a lesson card: trigger condition, observed failure, fix that worked, evidence links (video ids, finding ids), measured impact.

GATE to candidate skill: same class of critical/suggestion recurs in >=3 videos, or the user overrides the same default >=2 times, or a fix verified by a passing re-review is reusable beyond one video. One-offs stay as project notes.
DRAFT with the skill-creator template (when, prerequisites, process, numbers, rubric, pitfalls, good/bad examples) and status 'candidate', scoped to the room(s) where it fires.
VALIDATE statically: references resolve, rubric and pitfalls present, numbers inside schema ranges, no conflict with an active skill (if conflict, the new one must name what it supersedes).

TRIAL in shadow mode on the next N videos: run the reviewer with and without the candidate; compare critical count, slideshow/variation scores, revision rounds, approval-on-first-try rate, user overrides, and later retention.

PROMOTE to active when it improves or holds metrics on >=2 consecutive trials with no new critical class introduced; bump version, write changelog, log as capability_extension in the decision log, add to index.
VERSION with semantic versions: patch = wording/numbers within range; minor = new step or check; major = changed default or contradicted rule; keep every prior version for rollback.
RETIRE (deprecate, never delete) when it has not fired in a long window, is contradicted by user overrides repeatedly, or a trial shows regression; record the reason and the successor.
Feed the reviewer: every active skill contributes its checks to the room's review focus so lessons become enforcement, not just documentation.
do: Keep lesson evidence linked to concrete artifact fields (accuracy rule)
Prefer updating an existing skill over adding a near-duplicate
avoid: Turning a single bad video into a global rule
Learning from your own unreviewed output without user or metric confirmation
Letting skills accumulate without retirement

numbers.note: thresholds are analyst-proposed defaults, not OpenMontage values

checks: Every active skill has version, changelog, evidence and trial results
Every retirement has a reason and successor or 'none'
